arguments.issue: Did the trial judge confuse the insanity defence under s. 16 Cr. C. with the defence of self-induced intoxication under s. 33.1 Cr. C.?
arguments.claim: The trial judge confused the insanity defence with self-induced intoxication defence, so s. 33.1 should be disregarded and toxic psychosis considered a mental disorder under s. 16.
arguments.quote: In general terms, the appellant argued that the trial judge had confused the insanity defence under s. 16 Cr. C. with the defence of self‑induced intoxication under s. 33.1 Cr. C.
arguments.weak_spot: The other side would argue s. 33.1 Cr. C. clearly limits the mental disorder defence scope, preventing intoxication as a defence.

arguments.issue: Is toxic psychosis caused by a single episode of intoxication a "mental disorder" under s. 16 Cr. C.?
arguments.claim: A single episode of intoxication causing toxic psychosis must legally be considered a mental disorder under s. 16 Cr. C.
arguments.quote: The appellant’s reasoning therefore rests on the premise that intoxication can never be the real or underlying cause of toxic psychosis and that toxic psychosis must originate in a pre‑existing mental condition.
arguments.weak_spot: The other side would argue toxic psychosis from intoxication is not a mental disorder but a direct effect of intoxication.

arguments.issue: Did the Court of Appeal err in applying s. 33.1 Cr. C. to exclude the mental disorder defence?
arguments.claim: The Court of Appeal erred by applying s. 33.1 Cr. C. and limiting the mental disorder defence, contrary to legislative intent and dissenting views in Daviault.
arguments.quote: More specifically, the appellant argues that Thibault J.A. erred in writing that '[h]is submission would have the effect of rendering s. 33.1 Cr. C. meaningless and [disregarding] the clearly expressed legislative intent...'.
arguments.weak_spot: The other side would argue Parliament intended s. 33.1 to prevent intoxication as a defence for general intent offences.
